items.text: The resulting token overlap between BASEVOCAB and SCIVOCAB is 42%, illustrating a substantial difference in frequently used words between scientiﬁc and general domain texts.
items.why: Shows the overlap between general and scientific vocabularies.
items.plain: The new scientific vocabulary shares only 42% of its tokens with the standard BERT vocabulary, showing a major difference in word usage between domains.

items.text: This corpus consists of 18% papers from the computer science domain and 82% from the broad biomedical domain.
items.why: Highlights domain imbalance in the pretraining corpus.
items.plain: The pretraining dataset consists of 18% computer science papers and 82% biomedical papers.

items.text: The other two models that use the new SCIVOCAB are trained from scratch.
items.why: Identifies training differences between model variants.
items.plain: The two models using the new scientific vocabulary are trained from scratch, unlike those using the standard vocabulary.

items.text: Some light experimentation showed that the uncased models perform slightly better (even sometimes on NER) than cased models.
items.why: Notes a heuristic choice regarding cased versus uncased models.
items.plain: Informal preliminary testing showed that uncased models slightly outperformed cased models, even on named entity recognition tasks.

items.text: We found the setting that works best across most datasets and models is 2 or 4 epochs and a learning rate of 2e-5.
items.why: Reports global hyperparameter choices instead of per-dataset tuning.
items.plain: Training for 2 or 4 epochs with a learning rate of 2e-5 worked best across most datasets and models.

items.text: We did not ﬁnd changing the depth or size of the BiLSTMs to signiﬁcantly impact results (Reimers and Gurevych, 2017).
items.why: Ablates network architecture choices for frozen embedding models.
items.plain: Varying the depth or size of the recurrent neural network layers did not significantly change the results.

items.text: We did not perform extensive hyperparameter search, but while optimal hyperparameters are going to be task-dependent, some light experimentation showed these settings work fairly well across most tasks and BERT variants.
items.why: Discloses a lack of extensive hyperparameter tuning.
items.plain: The authors did not perform an extensive hyperparameter search, but brief testing showed their settings worked reasonably well across most tasks.

items.text: SCIBERT performs slightly worse than SOTA on 3 datasets.
items.why: Identifies datasets where SCIBERT falls short of state-of-the-art.
items.plain: SCIBERT achieves lower performance than the top-performing existing models on three datasets.

items.text: The SOTA model for JNLPBA is a BiLSTM-CRF ensemble trained on multiple NER datasets not just JNLPBA (Yoon et al., 2018).
items.why: Explains why a baseline outperformed SCIBERT on JNLPBA.
items.plain: The top-performing model on JNLPBA combined multiple neural networks and used training data from multiple datasets rather than just one.

items.text: The SOTA model for NCBI-disease is BIOBERT (Lee et al., 2019), which is BERT- Base ﬁnetuned on 18B tokens from biomedical papers.
items.why: Explains why a baseline outperformed SCIBERT on NCBI-disease.
items.plain: The top-performing model for NCBI-disease is BIOBERT, which was trained on 18 billion tokens from biomedical papers.

items.text: The SOTA result for GENIA is in Nguyen and Verspoor (2019) which uses the model from Dozat and Manning (2017) with partof-speech (POS) features, which we do not use.
items.why: Identifies missing features compared to the top GENIA model.
items.plain: The top model for GENIA uses part-of-speech features, which SCIBERT does not use.

items.text: BC5CDR and ChemProt, and performs similarly on JNLPBA despite being trained on a substantially smaller biomedical corpus.
items.why: Compares SCIBERT to BIOBERT despite training corpus size differences.
items.plain: SCIBERT beats BIOBERT on two biomedical datasets and performs similarly on a third, despite using a much smaller biomedical training dataset.

items.text: For relations in Sci- ERC, our results are not comparable with those in Luan et al. (2018) because we are performing relation classiﬁcation given gold entities, while they perform joint entity and relation extraction.
items.why: Notes an invalid baseline comparison due to task framing.
items.plain: The relation classification results on SciERC cannot be compared directly to prior work because this study assumes correct entities are given, whereas prior work evaluated entity and relation extraction jointly.

items.text: No prior published SOTA results exist for the Paper Field dataset.
items.why: Notes a lack of prior baseline results for Paper Field.
items.plain: There are no previously published top scores to compare against on the Paper Field dataset.

items.text: Given the disjoint vocabularies (Section 2) and the magnitude of improvement over BERT-Base (Section 4), we suspect that while an in-domain vocabulary is helpful, SCIBERT beneﬁts most from the scientiﬁc corpus pretraining.
items.why: Speculates on whether pretraining corpus or vocabulary drives gains.
items.plain: The authors hypothesize that pretraining on scientific text provides a larger performance benefit than using a domain-specific vocabulary.
